lead: A bipolar transistor is biased by a current; a field-effect transistor is biased by a voltage. The gate draws almost no DC current, so no resistor network can set a gate current — it must set a gate-source voltage V_GS, and the device's transfer characteristic turns that into a drain current I_D. Biasing a FET therefore means solving two equations together: the device curve (Shockley's equation or the square law) and the straight bias line drawn by the source and gate resistors. Every JFET or MOSFET amplifier starts here — a microphone preamplifier, an oscilloscope front end, the input stage of an op-amp.
prereq: You need: the load-line and Q-point idea from Chapter 2.1, and FET construction, the transfer characteristic and Shockley's equation from your devices course.

sections.h3: The gate voltage sets the current

blocks.text: A BJT's collector current is set by its base current. A FET has no such input current: at DC the gate oxide or the reverse-biased gate junction passes nanoamperes. The quantity the bias network must supply is a voltage, V_GS.

blocks.where: I_D is the drain current in mA; I_DSS is the saturation drain current measured with V_GS = 0; V_P is the pinch-off voltage, negative for an n-channel JFET; V_GS is the gate-source voltage in volts.

blocks.text: For an enhancement NMOS the square law replaces Shockley's equation.

blocks.where: K_n is the transconductance parameter in mA/V²; V_TN is the threshold voltage, positive for an n-channel enhancement device; V_GS must be greater than V_TN for any current to flow.

blocks.text: Each equation holds two unknowns, I_D and V_GS, so one equation cannot fix both. The second equation comes from the resistors. Any gate voltage V_G and source resistor R_S give a straight line on the transfer plot:

blocks.where: V_G is the DC gate voltage in volts (0 V for self-bias); R_S is the source resistor in kilohm if I_D is in mA. This is the bias line, and where it cuts the device curve is the operating point — the same meeting of a line and a curve as in Chapter 2.1.

sections.h3: JFET: self-bias, fixed bias, gate divider

blocks.text: Self-bias is the standard JFET circuit. The gate goes to ground through a large R_G (1 MΩ is typical), so V_G = 0 and V_GS = −I_D R_S. The bias line I_D = −V_GS/R_S passes through the origin with slope −1/R_S. It also self-corrects: if I_D tries to rise, the drop across R_S grows, V_GS becomes more negative, and the JFET conducts less, so a drift in I_DSS is partly cancelled.

Fixed bias puts a separate battery V_GG in the gate lead. Then V_GS = −V_GG is fixed and I_D follows from Shockley's equation directly. It is easy to solve but needs a second supply and has no self-correction. Gate (voltage-divider) bias adds R1 and R2 from V_DD to ground; the gate current is zero, so the divider is unloaded and V_G = V_DD R2/(R1 + R2). The Q-point can then be placed anywhere between V_P and 0 V.

items: Find V_G from the gate connection: 0 V for self-bias, −V_GG for fixed bias, V_DD R2/(R1 + R2) for divider bias.
Write the bias line I_D = (V_G − V_GS)/R_S.
Substitute it into Shockley's equation to get a quadratic in V_GS.
Solve the quadratic and keep only the root with V_P ≤ V_GS ≤ 0 for an n-channel JFET.
Get I_D from the bias line, then V_S = I_D R_S, V_D = V_DD − I_D R_D and V_DS = V_D − V_S.

blocks.text: The depletion MOSFET behaves like a JFET whose gate may also be driven positive, because the channel is already there at V_GS = 0. Shockley's equation still applies with a negative V_P for the n-channel type, so all three JFET circuits work unchanged. Divider bias is usual because it allows V_GS above zero, where the device delivers more current.

The enhancement MOSFET has no channel at V_GS = 0; it needs V_GS > V_TN with V_TN positive. Plain self-bias fails, since R_S produces only a negative V_GS and keeps the device off. The gate must be lifted by a divider, giving I_D = (V_G − V_GS)/R_S with V_G = V_DD R2/(R1 + R2). Equating this to K_n(V_GS − V_TN)² gives a quadratic; keep the root with V_GS > V_TN.

Drain-to-gate feedback bias needs no divider, only R_G from drain to gate. The gate current is zero, so V_G = V_D and, with the source grounded, V_GS = V_DD − I_D R_D. The bias line is I_D = (V_DD − V_GS)/R_D. It self-corrects: a rise in I_D lowers V_D, which lowers V_GS and pushes I_D back down. Two resistors set the whole Q-point.

Finally check the region. The device stays in saturation, where it acts as a controlled current source, only while V_DS > V_GS − V_P for a JFET, or V_DS > V_GS − V_TN for an enhancement MOSFET. If that fails, the bias line and the transfer curve no longer describe the circuit.

figure.caption: The parabola is the device and the straight line is the 1 kilohm source resistor; they meet at V_GS = −3 V and I_D = 3 mA, the operating point solved in the example.

spec.title: Self-bias point of a JFET
spec.aria: A downward parabola for drain current against gate-source voltage, from 12 milliamperes at zero volts to zero at minus 6 volts, crossing a straight rising bias line at minus 3 volts and 3 milliamperes.

examples.question: A JFET has I_DSS = 12 mA and V_P = −6 V. It is self-biased with R_S = 1 kΩ and R_D = 2 kΩ from V_DD = 20 V. Find V_GS, I_D, V_D, V_S and V_DS, and state the region of operation.
steps: Self-bias means the gate is at 0 V, so V_GS = −I_D R_S, that is I_D = −V_GS/1 kΩ with I_D in mA and V_GS in volts.
Shockley: I_D = 12 mA × (1 − V_GS/(−6 V))² = 12(1 + V_GS/6)² mA.
Equate the two: 12(1 + V_GS/6)² = −V_GS. Expanding, 12 + 4V_GS + V_GS²/3 = −V_GS, so V_GS² + 15V_GS + 36 = 0.
With V_P = −6 V the valid range is −6 V ≤ V_GS ≤ 0. The root −12 V lies beyond pinch-off and is rejected, so V_GS = −3 V.
V_S = I_D R_S = 3 mA × 1 kΩ = 3 V.
V_DS = V_D − V_S = 14 V − 3 V = 11 V.
Saturation check: V_GS − V_P = −3 V + 6 V = 3 V, and V_DS = 11 V > 3 V, so the JFET is in saturation.
examples.answer: V_GS = −3 V, I_D = 3 mA, V_S = 3 V, V_D = 14 V, V_DS = 11 V, and the JFET is in saturation.
examples.check:
import math
IDSS = 12e-3
VP = -6.0
RS = 1e3
RD = 2e3
VDD = 20.0
A = IDSS/VP**2
B = -2*IDSS/VP + 1/RS
C = IDSS
disc = B*B - 4*A*C
r1 = (-B + math.sqrt(disc))/(2*A)
r2 = (-B - math.sqrt(disc))/(2*A)
VGS = max(r for r in (r1, r2) if VP <= r <= 0)
ID = -VGS/RS
VS = ID*RS
VD = VDD - ID*RD
VDS = VD - VS
print(round(VGS, 3))
print(round(ID*1000, 3))
print(round(VS, 3))
print(round(VD, 3))
print(round(VDS, 3))

traps: Writing V_GS = +I_D R_S in self-bias. The gate is at ground and the source sits above it, so the gate is negative with respect to the source: V_GS = −I_D R_S.
Keeping both roots of the quadratic. The second root usually lies outside V_P ≤ V_GS ≤ 0, or below V_TN, and must be rejected.
Forgetting that an enhancement NMOS needs V_GS > V_TN with V_TN positive; a source resistor alone gives a negative V_GS and never turns it on.
Treating R1 and R2 as if they carried gate current. The gate current is zero, so they form an unloaded divider and R_G may be 1 MΩ or more.
Skipping the saturation check, or inserting V_P as a positive number in V_DS > V_GS − V_P.

quiz.q: Why does a FET bias circuit set a voltage rather than a current?
quiz.a: The gate draws almost no DC current, so no network can set a gate current; the controlled quantity is V_GS, which the transfer characteristic maps to I_D.

quiz.q: Explain why JFET self-bias is called self-correcting.
quiz.a: If I_D rises, the drop I_D R_S rises, so V_GS = −I_D R_S becomes more negative and the JFET conducts less. The current is pushed back towards its set value.

quiz.q: A JFET with I_DSS = 8 mA and V_P = −4 V is self-biased with R_S = 1 kΩ. Find V_GS and I_D.
quiz.a: Bias line I_D = −V_GS/1 kΩ. Shockley: 8(1 + V_GS/4)² = −V_GS, which gives V_GS² + 10V_GS + 16 = 0, roots −2 V and −8 V. Reject −8 V (beyond V_P = −4 V). So V_GS = −2 V and I_D = 2 mA.

quiz.q: An enhancement NMOS has K_n = 0.5 mA/V² and V_TN = 2 V. Its gate divider gives V_G = 6 V and R_S = 1 kΩ. Find V_GS and I_D.
quiz.a: 0.5(V_GS − 2)² = (6 − V_GS)/1, so V_GS² − 2V_GS − 8 = 0, roots 4 V and −2 V. Reject −2 V (below V_TN). V_GS = 4 V, I_D = (6 − 4)/1 kΩ = 2 mA, which the square law confirms: 0.5(4 − 2)² = 2 mA.

quiz.q: In drain-to-gate feedback bias, why does the circuit settle at one Q-point even when I_D drifts with temperature?
quiz.a: V_GS = V_DD − I_D R_D, so a rise in I_D lowers V_D and hence V_GS, reducing the current; a fall does the opposite. The feedback is negative and holds the operating point near the curve intersection.

quiz.q: A student solves a self-bias quadratic for V_P = −6 V and gets V_GS = −9 V and I_D = 9 mA. What is wrong?
quiz.a: V_GS = −9 V is more negative than V_P = −6 V, where Shockley's equation gives zero current, not 9 mA. The root is physically meaningless and must be discarded; the other root is the operating point.

quiz.q: Write the bias line for gate divider bias and define every term.
quiz.a: I_D = (V_G − V_GS)/R_S, with V_G = V_DD R2/(R1 + R2) in volts, R_S the source resistor in kilohm, V_GS in volts and I_D in mA.

beyond: Not for the exam. On an integrated circuit a resistor-accurate Q-point is expensive, so bias is usually set by a MOSFET current mirror or a constant-gm (beta-multiplier) reference; see Unit 5, Differential Amplifiers and Op-Amp Internals. Drain-to-gate feedback reappears inside self-biased cascode stages and inverter-like gain cells, which need no divider at all. How V_TN and K_n drift with temperature decides whether a bias point stays put, which is why data sheets plot them. Useful searches: MOSFET current mirror, beta multiplier reference, constant-gm bias, self-biased cascode.
